newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FEATURE - Milosevic tries to erase war legacy in election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Milosevic tries to erase war legacy in election.

text.p: Serbian officials on the campaign trail never speak of the dead or maimed, the war crimes, the hungry refugees or the plunging living standards.
As federal and local elections on November 3 draw nearer, there is no mention of the wars that tore apart old Yugoslavia and the disastrous results of a nationalist project to build a Greater Serbia.
The colours are bright and the message is merry in the campaign orchestrated by parties loyal to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, who wants to bury memories of a war that he himself ignited.
In the first election in rump Yugoslavia since the wars in Bosnia and Croatia ended a year ago, voters are being presented with Milosevic's post-war reincarnation as peacemaker.
Since a peace agreement was signed in Dayton, Ohio, last December, Milosevic has been steadily purging government ranks of nationalist hardliners who are no longer useful to him.
A media campaign blames bloodthirsty right-wing paramilitaries for wartime atrocities, not the Yugoslav army.
Ditching nationalists in his Socialist party, Milosevic has created a new vehicle called the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), led by his Marxist wife, Marjana Markovic.

Trying to appeal to disaffected Serbian youth with pop music and vague slogans about a better future -- "JUL is cool" -- JUL has clearly been chosen to replace the Socialists as the dominant party in the long-term, political commentators say.
Enjoying tight control over the media, the state-run economy and a large police force, Milosevic's coalition is expected to prevail in the November 3 polling, the analysts add.
"The question is only the size of the majority," Bratislav Grubacic, editor of a political newsletter, said.

Although diplomats say the federal parliament serves only as a "rubber stamp" legislature for an oligarchy ruling the country, the polls are seen as a trial run for crucial elections in the Serbian republic next year.
Milosevic's term as Serbian president expires towards the end of 1997 and the looming question is how he will choose to retain power.
If his coalition manages to secure a two-thirds majority, Milosevic can amend the constitution and transfer authority to the currently symbolic post of federal president.
If he falls short of that, some say he may even consider the post of federal prime minister.
Either way, he is known for playing short-term games to preserve power. A year is a long time by Milosevic's standards.
The name of the ruling party may change and its members reshuffled, but little has altered politically in Serbia and Montenegro since Milosevic rose to power in 1987.
While the rest of Eastern Europe shed its communist past and moved to privatisation in the 1990s, Yugoslavia is still in limbo in an undefined political system.
A five-party opposition coalition, ignored by the state media, struggles to get its message across through a few independent newspapers and at rallies across the country.
For the first time, opposition parties ranging from liberals to right-wing nationalists have managed to put up a relatively unifed front, scoring well in opinion polls.

As Milosevic's television network lauds him as the guarantor of prosperity and stability in the Balkans, the opposition is warning voters that living standards will decline further without fundamental reforms.

Opposition parties are focusing on the local elections and say they may win control of the capital Belgrade and other towns where dissatisfaction is rife because of high unemployment and unpaid wages for those who have work.

The authorities were clearly shaken earlier in Octobert when the popular former central bank governor, Dragoslav Avramovic, agreed to lead the opposition coalition. But within days, the elderly Avramovic mysteriously withdrew, citing health reasons.
Even without Avramovic, the "Together" coalition still hopes for a strong second place finish to puncture Milosevic's image of invincibility.
After the vote, Milosevic will be saddled with the daunting task of keeping the economy afloat until the republican polls.
A four-year old U.N. trade embargo against Belgrade was formally lifted last month after Bosnia'a post-war elections.

The United States has kept an "outer wall" of sanctions in place, blocking access to international financial institutions to ensure Milosevic keeps his promises to respect the rights of a large Albanian minority.
Belgrade will probably decide to sell off parts of state telecommunications and railway companies to foreign investors to raise funds for the cash-starved economy.
Economists say Milosevic is not ready for genuine privatisation because it would undermine the power structure he rules with supreme authority.

"Privatisation does not suit Milosevic and his wife," economist Mladjan Dinkic told the independent weekly Vreme. "If they lose that kind of control, they will lose the basis of their authoritarian rule as it is now."
